fullPassage: Yet rather than simply take such sources at face value, they read them “against the grain”. Like all historians, social historians draw from a variety of primary sources. Social history often emphasizes ordinary people rather than elites. ( ① ) Yet, in most places and times, non-elites lacked access to education and, thus, did not produce substantial amounts of documentation. ( ② ) Even when they did produce documentation, these materials rarely ended up in archives where they could be preserved and made available to researchers. ( ③ ) Because of such biases in the historical record, social historians have to be very creative in their work. ( ④ ) Like other historians, social historians analyze textual sources produced by government officials, employers, and other elites. ( ⑤ ) So, for example, a social historian will read legal documents not only for the “facts” provided by slaveowners; she will also examine the silences, interruptions, rumors, and other details that offer hints about the enslaved peoples’ attitudes and actions.
title: Social History's Hidden Sources
